title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport
subtitle: A modern UDP-based transport with built-in encryption, multiplexing, and connection migration
summary: QUIC is a transport protocol that runs on top of UDP and gives applications reliable, ordered, encrypted streams without TCP. It folds the TLS 1.3 handshake into its own, so a new connection can carry data after one round trip, and it keeps many independent streams so one lost packet stalls only its own stream. Connections are named by connection IDs rather than by addresses, so they survive a move from Wi-Fi to cellular.

plainLanguage.summary: QUIC is a transport protocol that runs over UDP and provides reliable, ordered, encrypted streams without TCP. tldr.problem: TCP and TLS together need several round trips to start, let one lost packet block every request on the connection, break when the client's address changes, and are hard to improve because middleboxes and operating systems have frozen them in place.
tldr.mechanism: QUIC runs over UDP, carries TLS 1.3 inside its own handshake, splits traffic into independent streams, and identifies connections by connection IDs instead of address and port.
tldr.outcome: A secure connection after one round trip, with no cross-stream blocking and migration across networks. It is the transport under HTTP/3.

today: QUIC carries a large and growing share of web traffic, because every major browser and many CDNs and large web services speak HTTP/3 over it. Open source stacks such as quiche, ngtcp2 and msquic make it usable from many languages. Its UDP basis also means some networks block or throttle it, so clients normally fall back to TCP.

hero.subtitle: A modern UDP-based transport with built-in encryption, multiplexing, and connection migration

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
QUIC is a general-purpose transport protocol built on UDP that provides reliable, multiplexed, and encrypted communication. It was designed by Google and standardized by the IETF as a modern alternative to TCP+TLS.

QUIC combines the roles of TCP, TLS, and parts of HTTP/2 into a single protocol. By running over UDP, it can be deployed and iterated on without waiting for changes to operating system TCP stacks.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC is a general-purpose transport protocol built on UDP that provides reliable, multiplexed (many streams in one connection) and encrypted communication. It combines the roles of TCP, TLS and parts of HTTP/2. Because it runs over UDP, it can change without waiting for updates to operating system TCP code.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
QUIC addresses several fundamental limitations of TCP:

Challenge
TCP Approach
QUIC Approach
Handshake Latency
TCP (1 RTT) + TLS (1-2 RTT)
Combined 1-RTT handshake (0-RTT for resumption)
Head-of-Line Blocking
Lost packet blocks all data
Only the affected stream is blocked
Connection Migration
Connection drops on IP change
Connection IDs survive IP changes
Encryption
Optional (TLS is a separate layer)
Mandatory (TLS 1.3 built-in)
Ossification
Middleboxes inspect TCP headers
Payload is encrypted and most header fields are protected
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC addresses limits of TCP. Its handshake takes one round trip, and zero for resumed connections. A lost packet blocks only its own stream. Connection IDs let a connection survive an IP address change. Encryption is mandatory, and most header fields are protected, so middleboxes (devices on the path) cannot inspect them.

sections.title: Connections
sections.content:
QUIC connections are identified by Connection IDs rather than the traditional 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port):

Connection IDs
Each endpoint chooses its own connection ID. Packets carry the destination's connection ID, allowing the receiver to identify the connection even if the sender's IP address changes.
Handshake
QUIC combines transport and cryptographic handshakes into a single round trip. The Initial packet contains a TLS 1.3 ClientHello, and the server responds with its crypto material.
0-RTT Resumption
When reconnecting to a previously visited server, QUIC can send application data immediately using cached session keys, achieving zero round-trip connection establishment.
sections.plainLanguage: A QUIC connection is identified by connection IDs, not by the usual source and destination addresses and ports. Each endpoint chooses its own ID, so the receiver can match packets even if the sender's IP address changes. The first packet carries a TLS 1.3 ClientHello, so one round trip does both handshakes. A returning client can send data at once using cached session keys (0-RTT).

sections.title: Streams
sections.content:
QUIC streams are lightweight, ordered byte streams multiplexed within a single connection:

Bidirectional StreamsData flows in both directions; used for request/response pairs
Unidirectional StreamsData flows in one direction only
Client-InitiatedEven-numbered stream IDs (bidirectional: 0, 4, 8; unidirectional: 2, 6, 10)
Server-InitiatedOdd-numbered stream IDs (bidirectional: 1, 5, 9; unidirectional: 3, 7, 11)

Streams are extremely cheap to create — no handshake is needed. A new stream is opened simply by sending a frame with a new stream ID. This makes QUIC ideal for protocols with many concurrent exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: A QUIC connection carries many streams, which are lightweight ordered byte streams. Streams may be bidirectional or unidirectional. Stream IDs show who opened them: even numbers for the client, odd for the server. Opening a stream needs no handshake. The sender just sends a frame with a new stream ID.

sections.title: Flow Control
sections.content:
QUIC provides flow control at both the stream and connection level:

Stream-Level
Each stream has an independent flow control window. The receiver advertises how much data it is willing to accept for each stream via MAX_STREAM_DATA frames.
Connection-Level
A connection-wide limit caps the total amount of data across all streams. Advertised via MAX_DATA frames. This prevents the aggregate of all streams from overwhelming the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC limits how much data a receiver must accept at two levels. MAX_STREAM_DATA frames set a limit for each stream. MAX_DATA frames set one limit for the whole connection. The connection-wide limit stops all streams together from overwhelming the receiver.

sections.title: Loss Detection
sections.content:
QUIC uses modern loss detection and congestion control algorithms:

Packet Numbers
QUIC packet numbers are strictly increasing and never reused, even for retransmissions. This eliminates the retransmission ambiguity problem that plagues TCP.
ACK Frames
QUIC ACKs report ranges of received packets (similar to TCP SACK) and include an ACK Delay field that reports how long the receiver held the acknowledgment, enabling accurate RTT measurement.

QUIC's loss recovery is specified separately in RFC 9002. It uses algorithms based on TCP's best practices but with improvements enabled by QUIC's cleaner design.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC packet numbers only increase and are never reused, even for retransmissions, which removes TCP's ambiguity about which transmission an acknowledgement refers to. ACK frames report ranges of received packets and how long the receiver delayed the acknowledgement, which gives accurate round-trip-time measurement. Loss recovery is specified in RFC 9002.

sections.title: Migration
sections.content:
QUIC supports connection migration, allowing a connection to survive changes in the client's network address:

How It Works
When a client's IP address changes (e.g., switching from Wi-Fi to cellular), it simply starts sending packets from the new address with the same connection ID. The server recognizes the connection and continues.
Path Validation
After migration, the server validates the new path by sending a PATH_CHALLENGE frame. The client must respond with PATH_RESPONSE to prove it controls the new address.

Connection migration is invaluable for mobile devices that frequently switch between Wi-Fi and cellular networks. With TCP, every network switch causes a connection reset and must be re-established from scratch.
sections.plainLanguage: A QUIC connection survives a change of the client's address. After a switch such as Wi-Fi to cellular, the client sends packets from the new address with the same connection ID. The server checks the new path with a PATH_CHALLENGE frame, and the client proves it controls the address with PATH_RESPONSE. A TCP connection would reset and start over.

messages.note: Transport parameters ride inside the TLS ClientHello

messages.note: Followed by 1-RTT[0] data, sent before the handshake completes

messages.label: Handshake[0]: CRYPTO[Finished] and 1-RTT[0]: STREAM
messages.note: Application data starts after one round trip

fields.name: Header Form
fields.desc: Set to 1 for long header packets.

fields.name: Fixed Bit
fields.desc: Set to 1 in this version of QUIC.

fields.name: Reserved Bits
fields.desc: Protected by header protection; must be 0 once removed.

fields.name: Packet Number Length
fields.desc: Length of the packet number field, protected by header protection.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version of QUIC in use; version 1 is 0x00000001.

fields.name: Destination Connection ID Length
fields.desc: Length of the next field in bytes (0 to 20 in version 1). The connection IDs, token, length, packet number and payload follow and vary in size.
